reasons: Lake identity gives case_name 'United States v. Moore-Bush', court '1st Cir.', date_decided '2022-06-09', and year 2022.
Lake citations select official cite '36 F.4th 320'; no disclosed parallel or neutral citation conflicts with the page.
The opinion repeatedly analyzes Carpenter, historical CSLI, wireless-carrier records, and the third-party doctrine as the cross-doctrine comparison point.

The opinion expressly says: 'We, of course, have no such issue regarding the third-party doctrine to address,' so the page's 'Related (cross-doctrine)' role is appropriately limited rather than direct.
residual_risks: This case should not be taught as a direct third-party-doctrine holding; the disclosed text supports only a Carpenter/CSLI analogy and distinction.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: Keep the role as related/cross-doctrine and avoid implying that Moore-Bush itself involved third-party-held records.

reasons: The Barron/Thompson/Kayatta concurrence frames the analysis under Katz and Carpenter's reasonable-expectation test.
The competing concurrence also addresses whether defendants had a subjective or objectively reasonable expectation of privacy, so the home role is well supported.

The per curiam disposition states: 'The district court order granting Daphne Moore and Nia Moore-Bush's motions to suppress is unanimously reversed by the en banc court. We remand with instructions to deny the motions to suppress.'

The Barron/Thompson/Kayatta concurrence concludes that the government conducted a Fourth Amendment search when it accessed the eight-month digital video record of the front curtilage, but would deny suppression under good faith.
The Lynch/Howard/Gelpi concurrence states that law enforcement's actions did not violate the Fourth Amendment and that continued pole-camera recording of public view was not a search.

Because the only court-level majority text is the per curiam disposition and the merits reasoning appears only in two three-judge concurrences, the page's no-binding-search-rule characterization follows from the disclosed opinions.
residual_risks: The page should preserve the access/use distinction: the search rationale in one concurrence focuses on accessing the created digital compendium.

reasons: The disclosed opinion repeatedly identifies the surveillance target as the home's 'front curtilage'.
The merits debate turns on whether long-term pole-camera recording of activities in that curtilage produced a Fourth Amendment search, supporting a related cross-doctrine Curtilage role.
The case is an en banc First Circuit Fourth Amendment search-and-suppression decision.

The opinion states that the parties disputed whether the pole-camera record was a Fourth Amendment 'search' and applies Fourth Amendment search frameworks including Katz, Carpenter, Bucci, and good faith.
residual_risks: The 'Key' role should be understood as key for the framework/open-question treatment, not as a majority rule that long-term pole-camera surveillance is or is not a search.

reasons: Lens A does not raise treatment/currency findings.
The disclosed lake identity confirms a published First Circuit case with official citation '36 F.4th 320' and court '1st Cir.', which is consistent with the in-circuit weight label at the case level.
residual_risks: The weight label must not be read to make either three-judge merits concurrence binding on whether the surveillance was a search.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: If displayed near the holding, clarify that the case is binding only as to the disposition/suppression result, not as a settled search rule.
